entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In this episode of Private Life, the actress Holland Taylor reads Renata Adler’s essay “The Perils of Pauline,” an expansive assessment of Pauline Kael’s film criticism from the Review’s August 14, 1980, issue. Taylor has been working on films, television, and Broadway since the 1960s. She is a nine-time Emmy nominee, winning once, in 1999, for her role as a judge on The Practice. She was nominated for a Tony Award in 2013 for playing Texas governor Ann Richards in Ann. 

Renata Adler is a journalist and film critic who was a staff writer at The New Yorker for four decades. Her books include A Year in the Dark (1969); Toward a Radical Middle (1970); Gone: The Last Days of The New Yorker (1999); and the novels Speedboat (1976) and Pitch Dark (1983), which were both reissued by NYRB Classics. 

Last week’s episode was an interview with Lucy Sante that discussed Adler’s essay and film criticism. You can read “The Perils of Pauline” and other essays with a subscription to The New York Review of Books, which, in addition to twenty print issues a year, gives you access to our full archive since 1963.

entries.title: From Fear Set Free
entries.summary: Humankind cannot bear very much uncertainty; to our dying day, we are all afraid of the dark. And so we perceive the world selectively, exaggerating the significance of particular things, downplaying others, and ignoring most of what bombards our senses, all so that we might be convinced, from now until bedtime, that we understand ourselves […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Humankind cannot bear very much uncertainty; to our dying day, we are all afraid of the dark. And so we perceive the world selectively, exaggerating the significance of particular things, downplaying others, and ignoring most of what bombards our senses, all so that we might be convinced, from now until bedtime, that we understand ourselves and our environment. We do this even in the best of times—in fact, without this selective ignorance, there would be no “best of times,” just the pervading fear of what comes next. Imagine, then, a situation where to this basic existential fear of the unknown is added the uncertainty of living without the law’s protection. Where you are subject to the latest despotic decree directed toward “your kind,” or to the whim of the police officer with his truncheon, or to the clerk behind her desk deciding whether to issue you a passport. And where they, too, are terrified by the whims of those above them.

Imagine, further, that the regime sees all this—sees the power of fear and learns how to treat it as a commodity that can be stockpiled and spent as needed. Such a regime could attain its ends by making only a small number of opponents suffer physically while leaving the rest in psychological torment, wondering if or when the blow will fall. Their fear is not of blind fate but of consciously directed power. Making his subjects aware that they live at his discretion, rubbing their faces in the fact that he owns their destiny, is a form of torture the modern tyrant seems to relish. It is the distillation of fear itself.

For Judith Nisse Shklar (1928–1992) this fear of being in another’s arbitrary power is the ur-human experience that modern liberalism was developed to stave off. Not to guarantee the exercise of our God-given individual rights. Not so that human cultural and moral capacities might develop fully. Not to make our societies more wealthy or egalitarian. There are schools of political thought that focus on these and other secondary qualities of liberal societies, complaining, with justice, when they are lacking. Yet such concerns can render us historically shortsighted and morally obtuse if they cause us to forget that the pursuit of the summum bonum is a luxury available only to those who have been freed from the summum malum of political fear. Liberalism, properly understood, is the political science of putting first things first.

Max Weber once described himself as being religiös unmusikalisch—religiously unmusical. Judith Shklar was, to an eminent degree, historically musical. Born in 1928 in Riga, Latvia, she fled with her Jewish family to Sweden in 1939 to escape advancing Russian armies. One year later, to escape the Germans, they crossed the Soviet Union by the Trans-Siberian Railroad, hoping to reach Canada by way of Japan. As fortune would have it, all visas from Japan were canceled by the US government while the ship was en route, causing it to be intercepted and its passengers to be put in a detention center in Seattle. There, the story goes, the Nisse family was discovered by Hadassah volunteers come to aid the Asian detainees. The women informed a local rabbi, who in turn made their plight known to a local newspaper, which published an article that got them released and sent on their way to Canada. These “adventures,” Shklar once drily remarked, “left me with an abiding taste for black humor.”

There is nothing humorous about her famous essay “The Liberalism of Fear,” which she published in 1989, three years before her untimely death. Shklar’s intellectual style here, as in her life, is that of a counterpuncher. In her eyes the best arguments for liberalism were historical ones exposing the bad faith and naiveté of antiliberals on the left and the right. Her first book, After Utopia: The Decline of Political Faith (1957), was a penetrating and at times withering examination of Romantic critics of the liberal Enlightenment, down to Catholic and existentialist thinkers of the postwar period. In “The Liberalism of Fear” she brought those criticisms to bear on more recent critics, including some left-leaning ones with whom she was personally quite close, such as John Rawls and Michael Walzer.

Right-leaning antiliberalism is a far more potent force now than it was three decades ago. In the 1980s there were still fruitful discussions to be had with conservative and neoconservative critics of liberal public policies and the ongoing revolution in social mores. But the basic principles of liberal democracy—the primacy of individual freedom, limited constitutional government, the public-private distinction, the rule of law, the impersonality of public offices, toleration—were never thrown into question by either side. In this fundamental sense, we were all liberals then.

No longer. Today, reactionaries on every continent pride themselves on a belligerent illiberalism, vaunting the muscles in their heads that have never been used. The parallels with the European interwar period do not need to be exaggerated to stir memories. So much seems familiar: Catholic integralists proclaiming the priority of God’s law over man’s, heads of state brandishing nationalist identitarianism like a talisman. Even futuristic fantasies of a purifying apocalypse preparing the ascent of a technocratic ruling elite now circulate in Silicon Valley as they did in 1930s Europe. Oswald Spengler’s cultural pessimism, Carl Schmitt’s authoritarian decisionism, Ernst Jünger’s “storms of steel” bravado—all these notions chime again like ancient bells. Their reissued books sell briskly.

Advertisement

But why? Of all the innovations of the modern age that one might identify as a threat to the human good, why would liberalism, of all things, top the list? Judith Shklar took this question seriously. What she saw at work in reactionary rhetoric is a fallacy which presumes that since liberalism is a distinctly modern political idea—monarchy, aristocracy, oligarchy, democracy, theocracy, and tyranny all existed in antiquity—then liberalism must be responsible for every aspect of “modernity.” In Shklar’s view, what the earliest liberals conceived of as a narrowly political doctrine became in the polemics of the antimoderns a bacillus that infected every aspect of human conscious and social interaction, initiating a decline from which we have not recovered.

The irony in this charge does not escape Shklar, who points out the obvious historical fact that, however well developed its intellectual tradition, liberalism has hardly ever been given institutional form in the West, let alone in other parts of the world. In post-revolutionary France, politics were dominated by generals, competing revolutionary movements, and monarchists until the Third Republic, whose anti-liberal opponents were swept back into power by Vichy. Germany’s one post-unification experiment with liberalism was depth-charged by the Nazis. Spain, Portugal, and Greece only fully escaped the rule of dictators in the mid-1970s. The US, despite the liberal principles embodied in its constitution, could be considered a formally liberal polity only after the abolition of slavery and the enactment of civil rights legislation in the mid-1960s. Great Britain alone among the major Western nations can claim to have had anything like a continuous tradition of liberal government since the nineteenth century. How, then, could such a weak political force have triggered a civilization’s decline?

It couldn’t have.

To point this out, though, is not enough. To defend liberalism in the current atmosphere one must also define it, or more precisely, delimit it. And not just to meet the challenges of the antiliberals. If they conflate liberalism with “modernity” in order to attack it, too many contemporary liberals and progressives make the mistake of associating it with “all good things.” They fall victim to a different fallacy: that if liberalism is good, then all good (political) things are liberal. There is a tendency—particularly in the US and Britain, where the socialist tradition has been far weaker than on the Continent—to speak as if the great progressive reforms of the twentieth century were nothing but logical elaborations and applications of purely liberal principles, rather than changes inspired by principles that complement but are not derived from liberal ones.

In “The Liberalism of Fear,” Judith Shklar set out to reclaim a narrow and defensible theory of liberalism by recovering its original problematic. On her rereading (and, at times, rewriting) of intellectual history, liberalism was and still should be a narrow political theory concerned with guaranteeing individual freedom. It does not presume a cosmology dictating man’s place in the universe, or a philosophy of the good life, or a path to individual and social salvation, or a path away from salvation. Nor does it harbor utopian ambitions of human “emancipation” writ large—quite the contrary.

Initially liberalism was developed as a response to the social breakdown caused by Europe’s religious wars, and its promoters insisted on religious toleration as a first principle—one grounded not in philosophy or theology but rather in a realistic view of human psychology and political history drawn from their own experiences. Their insistence on the distinction between public and private—wherever the line is drawn—arose from concern about concrete abuses of power and how to limit them with laws and institutions. Liberalism so conceived prizes above all the rule of law, placing it even above the principle of democracy. As Shklar put it in a truly memorable phrase, “liberalism is monogamously, faithfully, and permanently married to democracy—but it is a marriage of convenience.”

The same might be said of the doctrine’s relation to social reform. A liberalism of fear is the absolutely necessary condition of a decent society, the sine qua non, but it is not a sufficient one. Depending on time and place, on changes in human consciousness and material life, the ability of individuals to participate as full and equal citizens in a liberal republic will call for different things. Failure of governments to pursue those things is not a failure of liberalism; it is a failure of human charity and ambition. Nor is failure to achieve those ideals a failure of liberalism; some things prove impossible to achieve, and one must admit that. But one doesn’t know until one tries. A liberal foundation in the rule of law as a constraint on arbitrary power can and must be built upon, without threatening the foundation.

Advertisement

Shklar’s essay is far more timely today than it was upon its publication in the waning years of the Cold War, when liberal democracy appeared to be the only legitimate regime left standing. Today the knights of cruelty ride once again; they are brazen, and they have new apologists and champions. Thanks to the cursed blessings of the digital age, they are more closely connected in global intellectual, political, and even military networks than ever before.

Judith Shklar did not live to see these latest transformations, but none of them would have surprised her. Except perhaps the speed with which the sinister, grinning cruelty of liberalism’s new enemies has been adopted by a large portion of the American public, which chose a dim Caesar to sit at the pinnacle of institutional power. I have thought of her often over these past years as I have watched wrenching scenes of agents of the United States government not merely arresting illegal immigrants, which is lawful, but snatching them off the streets and sending them abroad without legal procedures, or entrapping them at government offices as they arrive to regularize their situations. Who among us will forget the screaming babies, the hysterical spouses splayed on the floor, zip tied, as they fought to keep their families together while menacing dogs growled? Who will forget the look of fear in their eyes and the cruel relish taken in their plight by the online mob? The summum malum, indeed, in red, white, and blue.

entries.title: Getting into Trouble
entries.summary: Almost fifty years after the Czechoslovak human rights initiative Charter 77 was first reported in the Review’s pages, Václav Havel’s own long-lost account of his imprisonment now appears in English for the first time.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In January 1977 the writer, dissident, and future president of the Czech Republic, Václav Havel, was arrested by the Communist regime for his part in organizing the groundbreaking Czechoslovak human rights initiative, Charter 77. After his release four months later, he wrote a detailed account of his time in detention and then hid it so well that he forgot where it was. In 2014, three years after his death, it was found among the papers of his close friend Zdeněk Urbánek. Paul Wilson’s translation of the report, the first in English, will be published this fall as Lost and Found: Hidden Notes on My First Incarceration. The text below is drawn from that account.

—The Editors

If the Czechoslovak secret police truly understood the events they so carefully monitor, they would have realized long before Charter 77 appeared that something like it was in the works, and they might have avoided the shock that the launch of the Charter gave them.

For Charter 77 didn’t just drop out of a clear blue sky. Its appearance was a natural outcome of the circumstances that gave rise to it. On December 11, 1976, several people from different intellectual circles came together in the shared belief that something ought to be done. Out of their discussions came the intention to write a declaration that would include a concise analysis of the state of human rights in our country and would conclude by announcing the creation of a permanent body concerned with this matter. This first meeting was soon followed by two larger sessions in which the text of the declaration was written and edited and a method of gathering signatures agreed upon.1

Our experience thus far had taught us that gathering a large number of signatures in support of such a declaration would have to be done with all possible dispatch because the police would find out about it in a matter of days and move to block it. Nevertheless we decided to gather signatures discreetly over Christmas, hoping that the attention of the police would be less intense during the holiday season. The technique of gathering signatures was worked out so that it wouldn’t involve any unusual activity, since the people who met for this purpose were in regular touch anyway and no undue suspicions would be aroused.

The plan worked, and by Wednesday, December 29, at 4:00 PM—the deadline we’d set for completion—all the signature slips (there were substantially more than we expected: 241) were assembled in one place. We immediately made several copies of an alphabetical list of the signatories and attached them to copies of the declaration. I was on edge all that day, quite pointlessly as it turned out, since as far as we could tell there was no indication that the police suspected anything. We conferred with friends on the next steps, drank some bubbly, and, satisfied with a job well done, went our separate ways.

At the beginning of January, despite our efforts to draw as little attention to ourselves as possible, the police began to suspect that something was afoot. It appears that they got their first precise information about the Charter declaration and the initial list of signatories sometime on January 5, from France, from the printing house of Le Monde, which was set to publish the declaration the following day. Now, of course, the police began to realize the significance and the extent of the matter, and we think that sometime in the night between the 5th and the 6th of January they mobilized a small team of officers, the first consequence of which was our notorious ambushing at noon the following day. We were in a race against the clock, and we lost by just a couple of hours.

On the morning of Thursday, January 6, Ludvík Vaculík and Pavel Landovský came to pick me up.2 We drove to our friend Zdeněk Urbánek’s house, where we got everything ready to hand over to the state authorities and to mail out to the signatories. Earlier that morning I had noticed a car with two men in it parked about a hundred meters from our home, but I hadn’t drawn any hasty conclusions. At Zdeněk’s, however, we knew with absolute certainty that we were under surveillance: a Volga police cruiser was parked a short distance from his building, and another vehicle was prowling back and forth in a small park just across the street. We now knew they would follow our every move, but we decided to stick to our original plan.

As we set off around noon, the Volga fell in behind us. We soon realized that we were being tracked by several cars and that we’d have a hard time shaking them. Even so, Pavel—out of some kind of chauffeur’s pride—tried to lose them by driving wildly around the Prague neighborhood of Hanspaulka. The only advantage we gained by these maneuvers was that we found ourselves momentarily alone in a side street where I was able to cram at least some of the envelopes into a postbox. While driving through the intersection just past the former French high school we found ourselves boxed in by several cruisers. Policemen piled out and stopped traffic from entering the intersection, then yelled at us to get out of our car. They put us in separate vehicles, confiscated our bags, and drove us off to their headquarters in Bartolomějská Street.

Advertisement

The ambush must have looked like a scene from a gangster film. Passersby stopped to stare, perhaps thinking they were witnessing a movie shoot, because amid all the uproar they could see the familiar face of Pavel Landovský. As the police were taking us away, I thought: This is a fine way to launch our struggle for human rights.

While the initial interrogations by the police were what you might describe as scattershot, done purely to get their bearings (they hadn’t yet decided how to handle the whole matter), on Monday, January 10, the interrogations became more focused. At that time my interrogator was a certain Major Hudec, a tall, relatively polite man with an odd, rasping laugh, not deliberately sarcastic but rather unpleasant all the same. I refused—as did all the others—to say anything about the Charter, and because Major Hudec seemed incapable of having an interesting discussion, we spent a rather gloomy time together, long periods of silence alternating with short periods of the same, oft-repeated dialogue, which went roughly like this: “If I do something wrong and I’m a man, I’m going to come clean! We’ll take an hour to write it up and you can go home! I don’t get you—are you a man?” “But I haven’t done anything wrong!” “If you haven’t done anything wrong, then for God’s sake just say so. If I do something wrong and I’m a man, I’m going to come clean! We’ll take an hour to write it up and you can go home! I don’t get you—are you a man?” It went on like that (in my plays I call repetitions like that “circular dialogue”) each time followed by silence. And then again: “If I do something…” Major Hudec hammered away at me for two days, for ten or eleven hours at a time, despite the fact that it got him nowhere.

At first I wondered how someone with such a lack of imagination could have become a major. But later it occurred to me that I may have been underestimating him: the sense of futility that radiated from him began to make me feel physically ill. My head ached, I felt dizzy, and I was constantly battling a strange lethargy that made me feel as though I were about to faint. Was that precisely what Hudec was after? He clearly had two possibilities in mind: either I would lose my nerve and spill the beans, or I would keep my head about me but then return home in the evening so beaten down I’d have no energy left for the tasks that awaited me—answering questions from the reporters phoning from Vienna, Bonn, or Paris for comments, or consulting with other Chartists, gathering information, and so on. In short, I wouldn’t be able to function as a spokesman for Charter 77. So Hudec’s approach clearly wasn’t as pointless as it seemed, though it was not successful: my nerves held out and I was able to carry out my evening duties.

On Tuesday evening Hudec invited me—as usual—to come back the next morning. So on Wednesday morning I showed up at the gatehouse of Ruzyně Prison and said that Major Hudec had summoned me, and the guard asked me to wait. I sat in the waiting room for half an hour, trying to comfort a woman who was in tears. At last the guard came back and told me there was no one by that name here. I asked if I was free to go home, and he merely shrugged. So home I went.

It was about nine o’clock, and at first I rejoiced in my unexpected freedom. But I was in a quandary: What was I supposed to do now? I had become so used to these daily interrogations that I suddenly found myself faced with a desolate and hopeless void. Should I sit at home and wait for them to realize their mistake and come and pick me up? Or should I grasp the opportunity and go into hiding? But where could I go? Other Chartists were either at work or in Ruzyně Prison being interrogated, and spending my time on anything other than the Charter seemed absurd.

Advertisement

Eventually I decided on a rather strange solution, somewhere between disappearing and flaunting my presence in broad daylight: I would go and sit in the Slavia café. (To explain: the Slavia had long been an important part of my life. I was a regular there for most of my youth. It was there that I experienced my literary beginnings, and engaged in endless, intense discussions with friends and fellow students. I even met Olga, my future wife, there. But it had been a good fifteen years since I stopped frequenting the Slavia, and I couldn’t remember when I’d last been there.) I sat by a window, ordered a coffee, and mulled things over. Slowly but surely I began to suspect that it wasn’t a mistake after all, and that the entire anomalous situation, when everyone but me was in Ruzyně, signaled something far more ominous: What if at that moment they were deciding to alter my status from witness to suspect?

The next morning the situation became even more ominous. Everyone else was being interrogated, but around me there was this mysterious silence. I was beset by a deep uneasiness again, and I went to a pub in Žitná Street to ward it off with lunch and several beers. At noon Jiří Němec showed up, along with Milan Balabán, an evangelical pastor and one of the signatories.3 We read the newspapers and analyzed the campaign they were waging against us, which was already underway: “outraged workers” were being quoted in all the newspapers and appearing on television and radio.

We spent that afternoon and evening in one of the “conspiratorial apartments” where meetings and consultations were taking place. We drafted a document about the education system; we assessed our situation and shared what we knew. At about 10:00 PM I decided to ignore my unease, go home, have a decent sleep, take a bath, and shave. We didn’t know whether they had already learned where we were meeting and had the apartment under surveillance—probably not—but that day everything seemed suspicious to us, and none of our precautions felt adequate.

When we left the apartment Pavel, who was supposed to drive me to my car, asked me to walk a hundred meters behind him. (The point of this escaped me, but I didn’t question it so as not to seem stupid.) He took a circuitous route—it was a part of Prague I was unfamiliar with—walked twice around the block, then somehow got far ahead of me and I began to lose him. I started running to catch up, but when he saw me running he began to run too, and suddenly we were both pelting like mad through the empty streets, and when we finally met up, quite exhausted, at his car, we were at a loss to explain why we hadn’t just walked together in a normal fashion.

At home I slept and then got up early because I wanted to have a quiet bath before they came for me. When I had finished my rather extensive ablutions, the doorbell rang, I answered it, and in the doorway stood Major Hudec along with two tough-looking fellows. He chuckled in his raspy fashion and said in a jovial tone, “Why, Mr. Havel, wherever have you been?”

He seemed to be admonishing me for not showing up at the prison myself, a not entirely absurd idea given how anxious I’d been over the previous two days. If I’d been able to follow my innermost feelings, I would have much preferred to bring the whole game to an end and turn myself in. My state of mind was akin to that of a man wandering through a city where on every street corner there is a “WANTED” poster with his face on it.

I asked Hudec whether I was being taken in as a witness or as a suspect, and he chuckled and said, “As a witness, of course.” Nevertheless I took the emergency toiletries kit I’d been carrying around with me for ten days, said good-bye to Olga, and off I went.

I returned 127 days later.

Perhaps it was on Monday—but more probably not until Tuesday—that a robust man with a lush beard turned up at my interrogation. (At the time I was being interrogated every day.) I gathered at once that he wasn’t with the secret police, not only because they typically don’t have beards but also because he wasn’t their type. The interrogators immediately got respectfully to their feet, while he more or less ignored them and offered to shake my hand, which rather surprised me. He introduced himself as “Dr. Fremund, senior prosecutor in the attorney general’s office.” We all sat down, and the new arrival began to speak. His tone was serious, he spoke to the point, and there was something soothing, even stimulating, in his voice. He began with a brief prologue in which he announced that I was being officially detained.

Then he briefly explained his reasons. Basically, he said that many foreign journalists were turning to me, as a spokesman for the Charter, and many more would probably do so, and that my statements were, he said, getting me into trouble, and it could be expected that I’d get even deeper into trouble, and so the feeling was that it would be better for me to be shielded from all of that for now, in case I eventually got more deeply involved, which would be very silly of me, particularly because those journalists often misrepresented what I said and twisted it in ways that turned my statements into attacks on the republic. Of course, it would certainly be possible to investigate my crime without locking me up, but it was in my own interest as well as the general interest that I not carry on as I had been, which is precisely what my being in custody was meant to prevent. Then he asked me whether I was familiar with my indictment and whether I wanted to say anything about it that he could add to his statement.

I said something along these lines, that Paragraph 98 of the criminal code assumes a person has acted out of hostility to the socialist system of government, but I didn’t consider myself an enemy of that system, and that what led me to do what I did was an attempt to contribute to its improvement.

Dr. Fremund said we didn’t need to add that because I had said it in my earlier statements, and was there anything else?

I said I was being accused of maintaining contact with some vaguely defined hostile centers abroad but that I had no such contacts.

Dr. Fremund said we didn’t have to add that because I had said it in my earlier statements.

Next he gave me a form to sign, and I signed it, thus acknowledging that I was officially in custody.

Then he asked me in a friendly tone if I had any requests, any particular needs, any complaints. I didn’t immediately know what to say, but then—if I’m not mistaken—I asked whether my wife could bring me some books.

Dr. Fremund said that unfortunately he had to disappoint me, but people under indictment were entitled to read books only from the prison library.

Then he stood up and offered me his hand, the interrogators politely got to their feet again, and Dr. Fremund asked them where he might find a comrade Horák. One of the interrogators leaped to the door and offered to take him there. Both of them left the room.

On the whole I have this to say about Dr. Fremund: during my stay in Ruzyně I met him a total of four times, and each of those encounters had one basic element in common. Each time the news he delivered was bad, but he delivered it in a way that left me feeling pleased, calmed, encouraged, if not exactly exhilarated. In short, the encounter always somehow created a moment of clarity in the general darkness that surrounded me in Ruzyně. At the same time, I knew very well that this man could never bring me any good news, and yet—as incomprehensible as it seems—I always, each time, succumbed to the calming effect he had on me.

I have often asked myself: What kind of person was he, really? In the whole anonymous machinery of the security and justice system, he stood apart: the full beard, those inconspicuous attempts at dry humor, the aura of comfort he radiated. And yet there was no genuine human warmth in him. His behavior was matter of fact, measured, official. What was he like at home? I don’t know why, but I can’t help feeling that if he wasn’t a confirmed bachelor, then certainly, as a husband or a father, he was one of those domestic tyrants with a lot of minor idiosyncrasies and peculiar habits that his nearest and dearest have to respect unconditionally, but for which they silently loathe him. At the same time, they yield entirely to some cold charisma in his personality, so that there is practically no chance for them to rebel. Even if he were married, he undoubtedly has in his nature some traits of a confirmed bachelor: a selfish clinging to old habits, the inability to be a real partner to anyone.

But whatever he’s really like, he is uncommonly well suited to his job. He has the ability to communicate anything to anyone in a persuasive and reassuring manner. I can imagine him arguing in front of a tribunal that I be given the death penalty, but doing it in a way that would leave me delighted with his speech.

I went through the release procedure that May in a kind of half-dream. Only six weeks before, I had been convinced that I wouldn’t see the normal world again for another five years, and now suddenly I was about to return to it. Naturally, I couldn’t stop myself from feeling elated, but at the same time I was trembling with anxiety, wondering how they might be preparing to stitch me up.

At about one o’clock the whole procedure was concluded and a guard led me through the Ruzyně Prison complex to the main gate. Olga and Zdeněk Urbánek were already waiting on the other side. I walked through the gate, and then an odd thing occurred: I felt that everything was just as it had been before, that in fact nothing had happened, that I hadn’t been anywhere, or had been away for only the weekend. The trees, the cars, the people, the sky—everything that I had missed so badly and that I thought would seem almost unbelievable when I saw it again didn’t surprise me at all. I took it all in my stride. It was as though my prison psychosis had utterly fallen away, and I behaved confidently and quite normally. It was only gradually that I came to recognize how my psychophysical state had led me astray—because for the longest time, I was anything but normal. The feeling I had was no more than a superficial mimicry of normality. The world in which I suddenly found myself again was so like the one I had lived in for more than forty years that it created in me the illusion that I, too, had not changed and that therefore I could go on moving in it the way I had moved in it all my life.

Olga and Zdeněk and I embraced (he brought me flowers), then we put my things in the car and drove off. And all at once I burst into tears. I was shocked, because the last time I had cried like that I was still a child. I apologized to Olga and Zdeněk, I said I didn’t understand it and found it terribly embarrassing. It did not fit with my illusion that I was calm and in control. “Some warrior for human rights,” I said to myself.

We drove home, carried my things upstairs. I was surprised at how colorful our flat was. We drank whiskey, I smoked the American cigarettes Zdeněk had picked up for me on the way to Ruzyně, and we talked about everything under the sun.

I couldn’t sleep, nor did I want to. All night long I read through piles of Charter texts that were waiting on my desk—documents, press releases, analyses, essays, documentation from legal workplace disputes, and so on. It made for thrilling reading, allowing me to take another step toward understanding everything that had gone on outside prison in my absence. I had missed the first and most important phase of what could be called the heroic era of the Charter. Now I was constantly amazed at how many smart, courageous texts had been written, how many things had happened, how the latent creativity of so many people had blossomed, and how so many people had grown. I was filled with admiration at how many didn’t simply sign the Charter and leave it at that but rather understood their signature as a commitment to doing real work.

Of course the regime had helped all this along by the enormous pressure it brought to bear on Chartists. In some ways everything on the outside was worse than I had expected: I had absolutely not imagined the sheer ruthlessness of the persecution (dozens and dozens of sackings, the rigged workplace trials, the expulsions from the Revolutionary Trade Union Movement, the constant surveillance, the forty-eight-hour detentions, the interrogations, the confiscation of personal documents, the cutting off of telephone service, etc., etc.).

It forced even those who generally felt isolated and so would not normally have stood up for themselves to do so. The bare necessity of self-defense led many of them to shed their last remaining inhibitions. They began to call things by their proper names, and thus they enabled the truth to come out fully. I was fascinated, too, by how a foundational principle of the Charter—the notion of diversity of background—had become reality. Without force or persuasion, different groups became imbued with the same spirit, while at the same time retaining their own identity. Protestants addressed their congregations; Catholics addressed theirs; former Communists spoke to their traditional partners. It was a chorus of different ideas, styles, approaches, themes, and ideas, and all of it with a sense of concord that no one had organized, all aimed at the same thing: a peaceful, civil, but uncompromising expression of truth, a persuasive defense of basic human rights and human dignity. (How different was the tone of all these texts from that of the official campaign against the Charter, with its hatred, hysteria, and vulgarity!)

I couldn’t take my eyes off what I was reading, and I wanted to learn as much as possible as quickly as I could in case they really did come to arrest me on Monday.

  • 1

    On the background of Charter 77 and the government’s wider attempts to suppress it, see Tom Stoppard, “Prague: The Story of the Chartists,” The New York Review, August 4, 1977.

    ↩
  • 2

    Vaculík (1926–2014) was a writer, one of Charter 77’s initiators, and the author of the autobiographical novel A Czech Dreambook (1980), which describes a year in the life of a dissident publisher. Landovsky (1936–2014) was an actor, playwright, and signatory of Charter 77 who lived in exile in Vienna from 1978 to 1989.

    ↩
  • 3

    Němec (1932–2001) was a philosopher and clinical psychologist, and one of the central initiators of Charter 77. He lived in exile in Vienna from 1983 to 1990.

entries.title: The Work of Math in the Age of Artificial Reproduction

entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
There are seven questions in pure mathematics deemed important enough by the Clay Mathematics Institute, a nonprofit foundation devoted to “furthering the beauty, power and universality of mathematical thought,” that each of their solutions carries a prize of $1 million. To date only one of these “Millennium Prize Problems,” as the foundation calls them, has been settled: the Poincaré conjecture. A problem in topology—the study of the properties of shapes that survive stretching and bending—it had been “open” for almost a century before it was proved in the early 2000s by the Russian mathematician Grigory Perelman. But on September 8 OpenAI announced that it had settled a second Millennium Problem. While Perelman had turned down the prize money (as well as mathematics’ most prestigious award, the Fields Medal), rejecting both the notion of celebrity for mathematicians and the conceit that credit should be given to him alone, OpenAI issued a press release. The company’s claim, still awaiting the community’s judgment, concerns the solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations.

Equations are compact symbolic expressions that say that two ways of doing something mathematically are equivalent. They are most interesting when there is something unknown involved, in which case a “solution” is the thing you “plug in” to give you the same thing “on both sides.” In this way, an equation gives you an indirect description of a mathematical object. A familiar one is x² + 4 = 5x, which says, “I am thinking of a number that, when I multiply it by itself and add four, is the same as if I just multiplied it by 5.” Only two numbers fit that description: 1 and 4.

A differential equation is an equation about change. In a simple example, it might be about some quantity changing with respect to time. Think of an infant on a playground swing. You launch her from a height and let gravity take over. She goes back and forth; at the highest points she stops for an instant and then travels back. As she moves back and forth her position relative to the center changes over time. She starts from “0,” then goes maybe a few feet behind, then a few feet ahead, and the corresponding numbers swing from positive to negative. Her acceleration also changes, and the farther out she swings the more strongly she is pulled back toward the center. The relationship between the position and acceleration can be encoded as a differential equation (including a mathematical caveat for air resistance). But here a solution is not a number. It is a record of the swing’s position at every moment, what mathematicians call a function. Drawn as a graph, it looks like a run of Formula-1 S-curves tapering toward a finish line.

When the unknown quantity depends on changes in more than one other factor—say both where you look and when (space and time)—then we have a partial differential equation. The traditional wave equation is one famous example with many applications. It even applies to a guitar string, when we consider the up-down displacement of any point on the string from rest. Here the wave equation encodes a relationship between that displacement and changes in the position on the string and the time since plucking it. At the beginning and end, where the string is pinned down, there is no movement. The closer you get to where you plucked it, the more it goes back and forth. Here the solutions include the famous sinusoidal waves that we associate with harmonics. Analogous equations can be written for a drumhead or the surface of a pond.

The Navier-Stokes equations, named for the French engineer Claude-Louis Navier and the Cambridge mathematician and physicist George Stokes, are also partial differential equations. They are foundational to a mathematical description of liquids and gases, and as such are essential to the study of fluid dynamics. A solution has two components: one function that gives the velocity of the fluid at every point in space and time (the “velocity field”) and another that gives the pressure at every point in space and time.

Like any good math problem, these have some conditions. The fluid is incompressible, meaning that whatever flows into a region must flow out. There is a viscosity parameter that gauges the “stickiness” of the fluid (molasses has high viscosity, WD-40 has low viscosity). Of course the fluid need not just sit there (it could, but that would be simple to describe), so we allow for an external force to generate the action. It can be strong and even violent in its effect, but it must be mathematically (and quintessentially) “smooth” throughout. Even the geometry of the container is idealized: we imagine that the fluid flows throughout three-dimensional space. No corners, no rough surfaces, free and unfettered, driven only by perfectly smooth Platonic paddlers.

Advertisement

The mathematician Leonhard Euler is generally credited as the first (in 1757) to formulate equations that model how fluid flows. The Euler equations are simply Navier-Stokes equations without viscosity. Euler later applied them to derive a model for blood flowing through arteries. In the early 1800s Navier tried to build on the Euler equations to create a more detailed description that accounted for viscosity. By the 1840s Stokes had cleaned up this attempt to give us the equations we use today.

Navier-Stokes is so fundamental—and provides such a good model of fluid dynamics—that we live its success every day. It underlies the mathematical modeling necessary for tasks ranging from weather prediction to airplane design. It is applied mathematics at its best: terse yet precise, as simple as possible, but not simpler, as Einstein would say. Its simplicity belies the difficulty of understanding the full range of what it encodes—that is, the full range of its possible solutions.

What makes the solutions especially tricky to figure out is a subtlety in their description: there is one “term,” like a phrase in a stanza or a chord in a measure, accounting for the fact that any flowing fluid at once moves with the current and makes the current. Think of a river. There are fast places and slow places, straight stretches and eddies. A leaf on the river—or leaves scattered about the river—materialize the velocity field. But we also have to remember that there is water moving through all this, effectively a continuum of infinitesimal packets of water both making up the current and riding the current. How fast and in what direction the water is moving therefore interacts with how the current varies from place to place. This gives the equations what mathematicians call a nonlinearity. It is also the source of turbulence, both mathematically and—for those trying to solve the equations—analytically.

For generations nobody could say whether the equations, starting from a perfectly smooth flow, could produce a point at which, in a finite time, the speed of the fluid becomes infinite. Such a “singularity” or “blow-up” would be a system spinning wildly out of control—and since real water cannot move infinitely fast, it would be the place where the equations stop describing the world. Resolving this lacuna is the Millenium Problem. It doesn’t keep us from applying Navier-Stokes in real-world settings, but it has been a nagging gap in the landscape of our mathematical knowledge. It now seems that we know the answer: despite the relatively innocuous-sounding assumptions, blow-ups can occur. The coincidence of simplicity of description and complexity of behavior is amazing, and surprising.

The story of the problem’s solution has by now been widely reported. In mid-August the NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and his collaborator Levent Alpöge, an employee of Anthropic, found a blow-up for a version of the Euler equations. Buckmaster and Alpöge built on the work of two Spanish mathematicians, Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa, who (building in turn on Martínez-Zoroa’s dissertation work) had by 2023 found a strategy to create a singularity out of an “infinite cascade” of nonsingular solutions, each one amplifying the effects of the previous ones. Buckmaster and Alpöge also used a range of large language models in their work. Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa used none.

OpenAI has a group of researchers studying the use of the company’s models for math research. While Alpöge and Buckmaster were working to finish a write-up of their solution, OpenAI heard rumors that significant progress had been made toward solving two of the open Millennium Problems. Not knowing which two, but now aware that the solutions were close, the company presumably saw an opportunity for their own research and business efforts. They put their latest, unreleased model to work on all six problems, along with some easier but still important warm-ups. Among those warm-ups were the Euler equations. After around fifty hours of compute time by nearly one hundred AI agents, they too came up with a solution that produced a singularity, which gave them confidence to go all-in on attacking Navier-Stokes.

To this task, by their estimation, they dedicated “on the order of” ten thousand agents. The agents were given the new Euler proof and centuries’ worth of published mathematical work. They very well may also have benefited from the residue of several years of mathematicians’ interactions with OpenAI’s wide range of tools. This swarm of agents was set up in such a way that they could efficiently share their findings among themselves—and share they did. They “talked” to one another for eighty-eight hours, generating 2.7 million messages—130 billion tokens of output, the equivalent of about several hundred thousand books of scratch work.

Advertisement

OpenAI’s human mathematicians oversaw the process, periodically using a second model to consolidate the most promising threads and feed them back. OpenAI has not said how much computing the effort consumed, but outside estimates put it at several hundred thousand GPU-hours, which translate to roughly the amount of electricity it takes to power a town for the four or so days that the model ran. Eventually the problem fell. The machine’s work still needs to be verified by humans, but initial assessments suggest that the problem has been settled.

The controversy over these results began as OpenAI strategized about how to make them public. The night before the company’s announcement, Buckmaster made a post on Mastodon sharing his and Alpöge’s achievements, including the Euler result. He included links to preprint versions of the work as well as supporting materials, the latter of which included a “Lean-4” version of their work that enables a computer program to verify their proof.

Also attached was a document giving his version of the timeline and process, crediting the early work of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa (whom Buckmaster recommended for a Fields Medal) and claiming that he and Alpöge had also made significant progress toward resolving the Millennium Problem. He apologized for the somewhat unpolished nature of their write-ups (“AI slop” is how he described the write-up of the Euler result), which he explained he had hurried out the door because he felt “pressured by outside factors.” The next day OpenAI issued their press release.

By Buckmaster’s account, he had reached out to OpenAI several days earlier, after word got back to him that rumors about his and Alpöge’s work were circulating there. He then, he said, had a tense back and forth with the company regarding how they had achieved their result and how they were going to announce it. Buckmaster had concerns that OpenAI had used work of his, which he had shared with the company by using its tools over the preceding months, never thinking that OpenAI was or would be working on Navier-Stokes. He alleged that in a phone call two days earlier an OpenAI scientist had offered him authorship on the company’s paper provided that Alpöge—an Anthropic employee—be left off. OpenAI denies trying to withhold credit from Alpöge (although it has said that it did want to bring only Buckmaster in as a coauthor). OpenAI also now claims that nothing Buckmaster typed could have reached the model. The company’s September 8 announcement credits both men, recognizes their priority on Euler, and says that it will not claim the prize. Whatever happened on that call, the episode cut against the oldest norms of scholarly credit and collaboration and fed the cynicism many of us already feel about the AI industry’s public professions of altruism.

Priority controversies are hardly new in academia, or in mathematics, for that matter, but there are greater stakes here. It is meaningful that the AI giants have chosen mathematics as the arena for a cage match. Mathematics is a touchstone of intelligence, even of genius, and there is no dispute about when a problem is solved. A problem that withstood generations of officially very smart people is, in this sense, the cleanest possible advertisement for a technology whose product is thinking. The machine that solved Navier-Stokes was not built to solve Navier-Stokes. That is the whole point of telling us that it did. What we are witnessing is a spectacle of computational power staged to acquire market share, and with it control of a landscape that extends well beyond mathematics.

OpenAI showed that the Navier-Stokes equations can “experience a singularity.” But did we? The model solved one of the world’s most important math problems. But it’s just a math problem. These are, for sure, complicated puzzles, some generated by thinking about the world around us and many that come completely from a world inside us, vistas on some elaborate ziggurat of the intellect that we continue to build. Solving them brings joy and understanding to a relatively small number of people around the world.

Unfortunately, the most important problems that we face are not math problems. Some, like climate change and even AI’s “alignment problem,” have mathematical components, but the most important problems are people problems, and no matter how much we might try to make them into math problems, they aren’t. Mathematicians have been solving long-standing math problems for centuries. If this were a sign of superintelligence, I’d like to think that at least one of these problem solvers could have brought more lasting happiness to the human race.

Did OpenAI’s model do math? Kind of. Mathematicians have been using machines to help prove theorems for over fifty years. Whatever the machine did here, however, it did not do it in the way humans would. One way to say what it did was that it “simulated” the act of doing mathematics—albeit to great effect. Any given piece of that scratch work might look like a dashed-off expression on a blackboard or an email between collaborators. And yet the process as a whole—a group of people serving up and organizing ideas for a machine—is, well, very un-mathlike.

For some problem-solvers, settling a question is perhaps the only point of pure mathematics. The focus on the goal makes professional mathematics seem like big-game hunting and the profession like a competition. That is at least part of what Buckmaster might have meant when he called OpenAI’s solution a “Deep Blue/Kasparov moment.” But there is also something about the human journey in mathematical research. For most of us the process is itself at least as important, even a source of pleasure in its own right: looking at delicate symbolic hieroglyphics, puzzling alone and with others over a complicated expression or idea, the simple satisfaction of thinking hard about something, turning it over purposely and unconsciously, marinating in a problem. Living with a problem. We talk to ourselves and we talk to others, and when everything finally falls into place we take our time to give a careful, bullet-proof explanation. A mathematics paper is a human activity, written, not generated. Asked why he had not used the new tools, Córdoba spoke for the collaboration that made the whole thing possible: “I don’t use AI. I have Luis.”

I am reminded of Walter Benjamin’s well-known essay “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction,” first drafted in 1935. It is a deep reflection on what the technologies of photography and especially filmmaking had done to the practice—the art—of image-making. In a deft rhetorical display he argues that, once mechanical reproduction untethers a work of art from its singular existence, society reaches a dialectical fork. On the one hand, photography and film can democratize image-making for all kinds of positive effects: good things can happen when everyone is an author, or even more, feels as though they can be an author. These technologies also “bring out those aspects of the original that are unattainable to the naked eye.” But with reproducibility “quantity has been transmuted into quality,” setting the stage for a battle between concentration and distraction. The result is to promote a public that, according to Benjamin, “is an examiner, but an absent-minded one.”

There is a political danger here as well. Ease of access, for Benjamin, is a form of sleight of hand—it gives the illusion of voice without transferring power or changing the structure of property ownership. This is a Marxist argument, which Benjamin wrote in the shadow of Nazism and the fascist takeover of Italy. At our historical remove much of it reads as prescient.

We are now confronted with machines that are able to produce things that we’ve historically viewed as works of thought. But do they reproduce thinking? The mapping of Benjamin’s argument onto such a question is not one-to-one, but the resonances are hard to miss. His central observation is that the technique of reproduction “detaches the reproduced object from the domain of tradition.” In its most quoted form this is the famous loss of “aura,” perhaps the essay’s best-known concept. It has nostalgic overtones but also points to new opportunity. With freedom comes possibility, art as a vehicle for political action.

We again stand at a historical juncture that threatens the “aura” of a long-standing human practice. One reading is that we are at a gateway to a period of rapid self-improvement and accelerated research, and soon to be released from traditional and increasingly irrelevant educational structures. Even proofs can now be certified by machines. Mathematicians—including Buckmaster and Alpöge—regularly advance their own research with AI tools.

But something has also been lost, and that loss cannot be taken lightly. Connected to the Greek word for “breath,” “aura” links to the body itself. Thought is human. “Aura” also speaks to the amazement that we should feel in the presence of creative work. Its loss suggests a marginalization of human activity and a disregard or even disrespect for the creative act. A proof only loosely attached to the people who spend their lives thinking becomes detached from the history of thought, and therefore from the foundation of meaning that it created. When a new technology untethers thoughts from their thinkers, we go from thinking for ourselves to thinking that we are thinking for ourselves. And because the aura has not disappeared but migrated, from the thinker to the machine, we are more inclined to believe what we are told, and ultimately to start valuing its “thoughts” more than our own.

Our thoughts are our own because they come from our cognitive processes, our biology, our history. No two thoughts are ever exactly the same. Now that so many of us pass our thoughts and ideas through a handful of common AI midwives, the many small singularities that were each of us collapse into a handful of larger ones. The wisdom of crowds becomes the wisdom of a few. Receiving the machine’s words in a room alone or wrapped up in headphones, we may experience them as our own ideas, but they aren’t. And the machines producing all those seemingly individual voices are owned by a very small number of powerful companies.

In the essay’s epilogue, Benjamin makes a direct connection to fascism. He reminds us of the Futurists and their celebration of the speed, power, and beauty of the machine. He quotes Marinetti, by then closely identified with Italian Fascism, extolling even modern warfare as an aesthetic triumph of technology. When speed and power become objects of admiration in themselves, the human activity they were supposed to serve becomes the slow thing, the obstacle. For Benjamin, writing in the interwar years, amid both memories of the technology-enabled carnage of World War I and the specter of fascism, the endpoint of that logic was war. Its’s not difficult to bring at least the first part of that analogy to OpenAI’s achievement: eighty-eight hours, ten thousand agents, 130 billion tokens, and one historic theorem. The announcement’s implicit message—intentional or not—is that humans are the past and LLMs are the future.

For Benjamin, this was a battle of aesthetics that ultimately played out on a real battlefield. Perhaps ours is also a battle of aesthetics that is now playing out in the environment, economy, and university. Whether we go on thinking for ourselves and with others—carefully and, yes, even slowly— when faster options are a click away is a choice. Sometimes the faster way is the better one. But sometimes you need Luis.

entries.title: A Plum Assignment

entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

The cover for our Fall Books Issue—a painting of ripe purple plums in a punnet, surrounded by hand-painted cover lines—was an unexpected collaboration between the Irish-born New Yorker Lena Beug, a commercials director, and the Canadian Jason Logan, who makes ink from natural pigments that he forages from rural and urban environments. 

I had assigned the fully illustrated cover to Logan, who was visiting New York at the end of August, and invited both Logan and Beug to dinner. While he was sketching ideas, she arrived bearing plums to cook the popular New York Times plum torte. The dinner table was covered in paint and paper, and Beug sat down and made some quick brush studies before starting to bake. After Logan’s first idea was rejected a few days later, he went back to the drawing board and made inky paintings of leaves and landscapes, hand lettering around the shapes. He then tossed one of Lena’s paintings into the ring. We agreed that it looked luscious. (The editors at first thought the punnet looked like a chair, but flipping the image solved the problem and the cover was decided.)

I wrote to Beug and Logan last week to ask them about art making, collaboration, and plums.

Leanne Shapton: Had you met before that afternoon in August?

Lena Beug: Never, but I have a tiny bottle of Jason’s ink on my tray of tiny, precious things. But we hadn’t met. I liked making a new friend.

Jason Logan: I feel like I have known Lena for years, but we just met that afternoon at your place.

Lena, you direct commercials for clients like eBay, Target, and Toyota, but what is your art-making practice like?

Beug: My practice is mostly just to make things, ideally without a lot of importance placed on the outcome. I have some complicated feelings about “Art” that may have something to do with being the child of a painter and having dropped out of art college, so it’s better if I just do it. I’m deep in a world of papier-mâché shells and pearls on my kitchen counter right now. I’m drawn to food and cute things like flowers and puppies and jewels and cake.

And Jason, what is yours?

Logan: I make ink from pigments I forage from sidewalks and wild spaces. My art is always a testing of the possibilities of the materials I combine. I particularly like hand lettering text, which is a place where word and image commingle.

Were any of the plums eaten before you painted the punnet?

Beug: Yes, at least one, I love plums.

Jason how was the plum cake?

Logan: The plum cake felt like that moment between summer and fall. A perfect meeting of sweet and tart, sticky and crumbly, light and rich, elegant and straightforward, with a dark plummy inside and a dusting of powdered sugar on top. Like an easy conversation with new friends.

I thought it was unusual, in this age of self-promotion and ruthless jockeying for attention, that I gave you, Jason, the assignment, but then you lobbied for trying someone else’s painting on the cover. Why?

Logan: I loved the look of the plums tucked into a basket. They felt right for the cover, itself an easy union of some of the best thinking and writing of the moment. The plums also embody something of the season, and of new friendships: playful painting at the end of the summer in a screened-in porch at a cottage on the water; pink wine and lobster rolls and yard-sale finds. The guilelessness of this leftover sketch on a scrap of paper won me over, beating out whatever needs I had for seeing my own artwork in the spotlight. I love what Lena made, I loved hand lettering around it with my favorite black walnut ink, and I loved working with Leanne, too. You always bring out the unexpected. The world has enough jockeying for attention, and not enough of whatever you might call this project.

Harmonizing?

Logan: Yeah.

Lena, your parents are longtime subscribers to the Review, what did they think of the cover?

Beug: The first thing I said when I found out about the cover decision was, “my parents will be delighted,” and they are.

You left your paintings behind after that dinner. Why didn’t you take any with you when you left? Were they still wet?

Beug: They weren’t wet, I just don’t need to keep everything. I like keeping it light. Also, as it turns out, if I had taken it with me, it probably wouldn’t have ended up on the cover.
